team.claim: Founders: Parker Conrad and Prasanna Sankar; Conrad is CEO. CNBC dates launch to 2016 and describes Conrad’s prior exit from Zenefits. Sankar’s current operating role is not established.

Company leadership roster as observed 2026-10-21: Parker Conrad, co-founder/CEO; Matt MacInnis, President/CPO; Matt Plank, CRO; Adam Swiecicki, CFO; Martin White, General Counsel; Stephanie Ho, SVP Customer Experience; Sunil Raman, SVP Business and Product Operations; Bridget Abraham, Chief Compliance Officer.

Company announcement identifies Albert Strasheim as CTO and SVP Engineering, previously VP Engineering at Segment; the current leadership page also lists him, but its extracted roster omits his title.

Self-reported notable departure within the review window: Chris Campbell announced leaving after five years as Deputy General Counsel on 2025-10-31. This does not establish a broader executive-turnover pattern.

funding.claim: Series D: Company announcement reports $250 million, co-led by Bedrock and Kleiner Perkins, at an $11.25 billion valuation. The opened page is updated 2025-06-19; the original financing announcement date is not established by that page.

Series E: Company announcement reports $500 million led by Greenoaks in response to the March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank failure. The opened announcement is updated 2024-03-26; distinguish that update from the financing period.

Series F: Reuters reported $200 million primary capital led by Coatue at a $13.5 billion valuation on 2024-04-22. A separate tender offer contemplated up to $590 million for employees and early investors; this was not additional primary capital.

Series G: Company announced $450 million primary financing on 2025-05-09 at a $16.8 billion valuation, naming Elad Gil, Sands Capital, GIC, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Baillie Gifford and Y Combinator among investors. It separately signed agreements for up to $200 million of employee/former-employee equity repurchases; completion of the full amount is not established.
Latest valuation located: CNBC’s 2026-05-19 profile still identifies the May 2025 Series G and $16.8 billion valuation as the latest financing benchmark; this is not a live October 2026 valuation.
TechCrunch reported cumulative funding of $1.85 billion as of 2025-05-09; press-reported total, not audited capitalization.

output.verdict: Rippling merits deeper diligence: its integrated product breadth, named customer references and substantial institutional financing are credible strengths, while reported growth is promising but unaudited. Before investing, reconcile the conflicting revenue timelines and obtain current financials, customer-retention evidence and counsel’s assessment of the Deel litigation and surviving counterclaims.

business.claim: Company claim: Workforce-management software unifies HR, IT and finance around employee data, including payroll, recruiting, device management and expenses; buyers are businesses and their HR, IT and finance teams.

Company claim: Modular pricing depends on products and employee count; most products are priced per employee per month. Advertised plans start at $8 per employee per month plus a monthly base fee, as observed 2026-10-21; actual pricing requires a quote.

Company claim: Serves businesses ranging from a single employee to thousands across multiple countries; global workforce offerings cover hiring and payroll in 185+ countries and 50+ currencies, as observed 2026-10-21. Coverage is product-specific, not a claim of native payroll in every country.

traction.claim: Company claim: More than 30,000 customers, as observed 2026-10-21 on a comparison page referencing September 2026 information.
TechCrunch reported more than 20,000 customers as of 2025-05-09; this is an earlier snapshot, not the current customer count.

Company claim: Official customer stories name Chess.com, Kleiner Perkins, Dude Wipes, NinjaTech AI, The Channel Company and Clariti; these are references, not evidence of contract size or retention. Observed 2026-10-21.
TechCrunch reported Y Combinator became a customer in early 2025; company claims cited in that article also name Cursor, Clay and Sierra as customers.

Partner claim: Sequoia’s compensation-and-benefits partnership integrates its offering with Rippling HCM and benefits administration. This is Sequoia the benefits adviser, not Sequoia Capital; observed 2026-10-21.
Company claim, reported by CNBC: Conrad said in April 2026 that revenue was growing 78% year over year and that growth had accelerated for three consecutive quarters; not audited results.

red_flags.claim: Litigation and competitive-conduct risk: active reciprocal claims include surviving advertising allegations. Obtain counsel’s current case assessment, discovery obligations, insurance coverage and estimated exposure; the cited order establishes procedural risk, not liability.

Financial-quality risk: the published $1 billion ARR timing is not supported here by audited accounts and conflicts with the separately cited annualized-revenue estimate. Reconcile ARR definitions, growth, recurring versus transactional revenue, cash burn and unit economics before underwriting.

Retention/execution diligence trigger: Glassdoor reports a declining employee rating and workload complaints. Test attrition, regretted departures and support staffing directly; anonymous reviews alone cannot prove a systemic problem.

Service-quality diligence trigger: BBB complaints include billing, cancellation and support issues. Validate severity against ticket volumes, payroll accuracy, retention and customer references rather than extrapolating from complaint anecdotes.

reputation.claim: Employee-review aggregator Glassdoor, observed 2026-10-21: 3.6/5 across 1,300 anonymous reviews, 66% recommend, and 80% CEO approval. Glassdoor says the overall rating declined 4% over the preceding twelve months; self-selected reviews are not an audited employee survey.

Anonymous employee-review themes include workload, burnout, management and work-life-balance concerns, alongside positive comments about colleagues, learning and product quality; these are reviewer opinions, not verified employment findings.

BBB complaint aggregator, observed 2026-10-21: 80 complaints over the preceding three years and 35 closed in the preceding twelve months. Records include cancellation, billing, onboarding and support complaints; complaint counts lack a customer-volume denominator and do not establish wrongdoing.

Critical press exposure: CNBC describes the contested Deel litigation and reports a criminal investigation into Deel. That report must not be mischaracterized as a criminal investigation or finding against Rippling.

financial_signals.claim: CNBC reported that ARR crossed $1 billion in 2025, in its 2026-05-19 profile. No audited financial statement was supplied; the timing conflicts with the separately cited Sacra estimate and requires reconciliation.

Third-party research estimate: Sacra estimates $1 billion annualized revenue in March 2026, versus $850 million at year-end 2025, and 78% year-over-year growth. These are Sacra estimates, not company financial disclosures; annualized revenue should not automatically be treated as audited ARR.

TechCrunch, citing sources who spoke to The Information, reported $570 million annualized revenue around 2025-05-09. This is a press-reported estimate, not an audited or directly disclosed company figure.

TechCrunch reported more than 4,000 employees as of 2025-05-09. The Series G company announcement separately said it was hiring across all roles; no verified current headcount or like-for-like trend is established.

legal_and_regulatory.claim: Exact litigating entity: People Center, Inc., popularly known as Rippling, in N.D. California case 25-cv-02576-CRB. Rippling sued Deel and executives in March 2025 over alleged corporate espionage. These are allegations, not established theft or liability.
The court’s order dated 2026-02-23 allowed most of Rippling’s claims, including RICO, to proceed at the pleading stage. Plausibility is not a finding that the alleged conduct occurred.

Deel asserted counterclaims against Rippling, Conrad and former employee Keith O’Brien. The 2026-09-25 order partly granted and partly denied dismissal, compelled arbitration and denied a motion to strike; some comparative-advertising claims survived. No final merits resolution is established by this order.

The 2026-09-25 order discusses contested Russia/sanctions-related statements and commercial conduct in the parties’ dispute. This is civil litigation, not a regulator finding that Rippling violated sanctions; regulatory exposure remains unresolved.

input: Write a due diligence memo on Rippling
